title: Assessment Modifications
description: Modifications to how a student is assessed — alternate methods, modified rubrics, alternate state assessments. Use when standard assessment cannot accurately measure the student's learning. Distinguishes 'on-demand testing with accommodations' from 'alternate assessment' as defined by IDEA.

source.name: Composite — Wikipedia (IEP, Special Education) and IEP form template (Massachusetts)
source.section: State and District-Wide Assessments and Accommodations; Modifications

modifications.text: Score the student's work on a different rubric than peers' (e.g., assess content accuracy and reasoning, not spelling and mechanics, when the IEP identifies a writing-mechanics deficit but content goals are at grade level).

Lower the criteria for academic success on a specific assessment. Example: rather than requiring 90% mastery on a math fact assessment, accept 70% as evidence of progress for a student with long-term retrieval deficits.

Substitute the assessment format. Examples: oral exam in place of written; demonstration in place of test; portfolio in place of single-test summative; teacher observation/checklist in place of written test.

For students with the most significant cognitive disabilities, the IEP may indicate participation in an alternate state assessment (e.g., MCAS-Alt in Massachusetts) instead of the standard on-demand state test. This is a high-stakes IEP team decision; not within scope of single-lesson modification.

Assess the student against off-grade-level standards documented in the IEP. Example: an 8th-grader reading at a 4th-grade level may be assessed against 4th-grade reading standards in modified IEP-aligned assessment, while remaining in grade-level instruction with accommodations.

Reduce the number of items on a test (e.g., 5 of 10 spelling words, 10 of 20 math problems). When the student demonstrates mastery on the reduced set, full mastery is inferred. Distinct from extra time — this is a content modification.

Remove time pressure entirely (not just extended time). For students whose anxiety or processing-speed deficit makes any time limit performance-altering, allow the assessment to be completed without a time cap.
Break a single test into segments administered across multiple days. Reduces fatigue effects and gives the student multiple windows of best performance.

Allow open-book, open-note, or word-bank-provided format on assessments where rote memorization is not the learning objective. Compensates for long-term retrieval deficits while still measuring application/analysis skills.

guardrails.text: Most state assessment accommodations and modifications must be pre-documented in the IEP's 'State and District-Wide Assessments' section. Adding a new assessment modification without IEP authorization may invalidate the score.

The IEP-listed MCAS (or state-test) accommodations should be mirrored in classroom assessments. If a student gets text-to-speech on MCAS, they should get text-to-speech on classroom tests too — otherwise the test score and the classroom data don't align.

Validity rule: an accommodation is valid if it changes how the student accesses or responds, not what's measured. A modification changes what's measured. Be explicit about which is which when proposing assessment changes — the distinction matters legally and academically.
